clinicalPearls: Cancer-associated retinopathy (CAR) causes subacute, painless, usually bilateral though often asymmetric visual loss with photosensitivity, shimmering photopsiae, ring scotomata and impaired colour vision.
Melanoma-associated retinopathy (MAR) typically arises in a patient with known cutaneous melanoma and presents with night blindness and shimmering photopsiae with relatively preserved acuity.
CAR is most often linked to small-cell lung carcinoma and to gynaecological and breast cancers, with anti-recoverin and anti-alpha-enolase antibodies.
MAR is caused by antibodies against retinal ON-bipolar cells (including TRPM1) and correlates with metastatic melanoma.

The full-field electroretinogram is the key test: CAR shows reduced a- and b-waves (photoreceptor dysfunction) whereas MAR shows a selectively reduced b-wave with a preserved a-wave, producing an electronegative waveform.
The fundus is frequently normal early, with later arteriolar attenuation, retinal pigment epithelial mottling and optic disc pallor.
In CAR the visual symptoms may precede the cancer diagnosis, prompting a systemic malignancy search.
Response to immunosuppression is generally limited and visual recovery is often incomplete.
reference.pathophysiology: Circulating antibodies directed against retinal antigens shared by the tumour trigger photoreceptor or bipolar cell injury. In cancer-associated retinopathy, antibodies against recoverin and alpha-enolase promote calcium-dependent photoreceptor apoptosis. In melanoma-associated retinopathy, antibodies against ON-bipolar cell antigens such as TRPM1 impair signal transmission from photoreceptors to bipolar cells, explaining the selective b-wave loss on electroretinography. The resulting outer retinal and bipolar dysfunction produces progressive, often irreversible visual impairment.
additionalDifferentials: retinitis pigmentosa and other inherited retinal dystrophies
additionalInvestigations: full-field electroretinography to characterise photoreceptor versus ON-bipolar dysfunction
serum anti-retinal antibody panel (anti-recoverin, anti-alpha-enolase and others)
optical coherence tomography of the outer retinal layers
automated perimetry for scotomata and field constriction
whole-body FDG-PET/CT and CT chest for occult malignancy
dermatological review and imaging for melanoma when MAR is suspected
redFlags: a known or newly suspected melanoma or lung carcinoma
electronegative electroretinogram indicating bipolar cell dysfunction
reference.prognosis: Visual prognosis is often poor; cancer-associated retinopathy tends to be progressive, while melanoma-associated retinopathy is more variable. Tumour treatment and immunosuppression have limited efficacy in restoring vision.
pitfalls: Mistaking the presentation for retinitis pigmentosa and missing the paraneoplastic cause.
Being falsely reassured by a normal-appearing fundus in the early stages.
Failing to order electroretinography, which is central to the diagnosis.
Overlooking a history of melanoma in a patient presenting with night blindness.
references: Adamus G. Autoantibody targets and their significance in autoimmune retinopathies.
